newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia communists to decide budget stance Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: Russia communists to decide budget stance Tuesday.

text.p: Russia's communists will decide on Tuesday what to do about the latest 1997 budget draft, but have their own ideas about the ideal shape of the spending plans, Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov said on Monday.
Zyuganov, speaking to reporters after a meeting with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, said he had given the premier his proposals. "He said he would examine them," Zyuganov said.
"Our group will decide tomorrow about its attitude to the budget. We have our own idea on its basic parameters."

The budget, crucial for the release of 1997 funds promised to Russia by the International Monetary Fund, has already been rejected once by the State Duma lower house of parliament, which is dominated by Zyuganov's communists and other conservatives.
Parliament is due to debate a revised draft this week.

Deputies, some of whom say Russia should print money to ease the pain of reforms, said when they first rejected the budget that revenue targets were unrealistic and the government was not doing enough to protect the poor.
Deputies and government officials then drew up a compromise budget but a senior parliamentarian warned on Monday the new plans had little chance of being passed.
The compromise draft sets spending of 497 trillion roubles ($85 billion) and a deficit of 95 trillion, equal to 3.5 percent of gross domestic product.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted Duma budget committee deputy chairman Gennady Kulik as saying parliament would not approve the compromise and "only a miracle" could rescue it.
Kulik, a member of the conservative Agrarian Party, urged the government to find new ways to bring in revenue and use central bank credits to help fund the deficit.
The government, following what it describes as non-inflationary recipes to close the budget gap, has vowed not to use central bank loans.
But Kulik said there was no need to worry about cash emission if the money was used to fund construction programmes and help industrial development.
Richard Layard, a British analyst who has been following the Russian economy closely, disagreed.

"I think the one solid achievement of recent years has been the elimination of inflation," he told a news conference. "Probably the greatest tragedy would be if Russia were to go back to printing money."
If the Duma rejects the budget, the government will be required to rework it within 20 days, making it very unlikely that parliament could approve the plan before the end of 1996.
The government would then either use spending patterns from the 1996 budget or survive with quarterly budgets until a law on spending plans for the whole year was passed.
